note: The SpacetimeDB counterpart to postgres-l1-authz.json. Validating the new
criteria against only one backend would tell us the grader catches defects
in that backend's shape — which is the bias worth avoiding, since the point
of the benchmark is a fair comparison.
These edit the MODULE, so they need a republish rather than a hot reload.
The runner republishes through the authenticated backend lease during each
reset and republishes the restored source before it exits the mutant.
EXPECTATION, recorded before running so the result cannot be rationalised
afterwards:
- leak-every-message SHOULD be caught. The view is the subscription, so
dropping its filter puts other people's direct messages on the wire while
the interface still renders only the open conversation.
- anyone-can-remove-a-member is EXPECTED TO SURVIVE, and that is a known
hole rather than a pass. Authorization is verified by re-issuing a real
request as the wrong user, and a reducer call cannot be replayed over
HTTP — so on this backend the criterion rests on its DOM assertion, which
a server-side change does not affect. If it survives, the honest reading
is that the harness cannot currently see server-side authorization holes
on SpacetimeDB, NOT that SpacetimeDB has none. Fixing it means driving the
reducer from the wrong actor's own live connection.

mutations.desc: The my_messages view stops restricting rows to conversations the caller belongs to, so every client is sent every message including other people's direct ones. The interface still shows only the open conversation.
The ownership check in the removeMember reducer is dropped. The control stays hidden from non-owners, so nothing visible changes.
mutations.find: if (!myMembership || !myMembership.isOwner) throw new SenderError('only an owner can remove members');
mutations.replace: if (false) throw new SenderError('only an owner can remove members');
